lessons.title: From Congress to Independence, 1774–76
lessons.description: Continental Congresses, Paine’s ‘Common Sense’ and the Declaration of 1776.
lessons.content_html:
Reconciliation Was Still the Goal in 1774

When delegates from twelve colonies (Georgia stayed away) gathered at Philadelphia in September 1774, almost none of them wanted independence. They wanted the Intolerable Acts repealed and the constitutional relationship of 1763 restored. The shift from that goal to the Declaration of Independence took less than two years and was anything but predictable. Battlefield events, the king’s response and a single forty-page pamphlet all played a role. The lesson’s central skill is causation: showing why a movement that began by petitioning the Crown in 1774 ended up rejecting the Crown altogether in July 1776.

Key Fact

The First Continental Congress met at Philadelphia in September–October 1774. Twelve colonies sent delegates (Georgia did not). It produced a Declaration of Rights and Grievances and the Continental Association — a coordinated boycott of British imports enforced by local committees of inspection.

The First Continental Congress, 1774

The First Continental Congress sat at Carpenters’ Hall in Philadelphia from 5 September to 26 October 1774. Fifty-six delegates attended, including conservatives like John Dickinson and Joseph Galloway who hoped for reconciliation, and radicals like John Adams and Patrick Henry who already suspected war was coming. The Congress did three things. First, it issued a Declaration of Rights and Grievances objecting to the Intolerable Acts and to taxation without representation, but explicitly accepting Parliament’s right to regulate trade. Second, it set up the Continental Association: a colony-wide non-importation, non-consumption and (from September 1775) non-exportation boycott of British trade, enforced by local committees of inspection. Third, it agreed to meet again in May 1775 if grievances were not resolved. The mood was firm but cautious. Galloway’s plan for an American Parliament under the Crown was rejected by a single vote, but only just — reconciliation was still on the table.

Lexington, Concord and the Second Congress, 1775

The next ten months hardened the conflict. On 19 April 1775 General Thomas Gage sent 700 redcoats from Boston to seize a colonial arms cache at Concord. Massachusetts militia met them on Lexington Green and at Concord Bridge. By the time the British column straggled back to Boston, 73 of its men were dead and around 95 were wounded. The Massachusetts militia laid siege to Boston the next day. When the Second Continental Congress reconvened at Philadelphia on 10 May 1775 it was already a wartime government. It appointed George Washington commander-in-chief of a Continental Army on 15 June 1775. It also tried one last gesture of reconciliation: the Olive Branch Petition of July 1775, which addressed George III directly and asked him to call off his ministers. The king refused even to receive it and in August declared the colonies in rebellion. By December 1775 Parliament’s Prohibitory Act stopped trade with the rebellious colonies and authorised the seizure of American ships — in effect putting the colonies outside the king’s protection. Many colonists later said that this was the moment they accepted that independence was inevitable.

A common student error is to write the Revolution as a foregone conclusion from the Stamp Act onwards. The First Continental Congress’s Declaration of Rights and Grievances, the Olive Branch Petition of July 1775 and Galloway’s near-successful plan for an American Parliament under the Crown all show that reconciliation was still the majority position deep into 1775. The shift to independence was contingent on three things that did not have to happen: George III’s refusal to receive the Olive Branch Petition, the Prohibitory Act of December 1775, and the publication of Paine’s ‘Common Sense’ in January 1776. Higher-band analytical-narrative answers explain how these contingent events converted opinion; lower-band answers treat the outcome as inevitable.

Thomas Paine’s ‘Common Sense’, January 1776

In January 1776 the English-born radical writer Thomas Paine published a forty-page pamphlet called ‘Common Sense’. It sold around 120,000 copies in three months and perhaps 500,000 over the year — in a colonial population of roughly 2.5 million. Paine did three things no previous patriot writer had done. He attacked monarchy itself rather than the king’s ministers, calling George III the ‘Royal Brute of Britain’. He framed independence as common sense rather than radical revolution — America was a continent, not a province. And he wrote in plain English aimed at farmers, sailors and tradesmen rather than lawyers and assemblymen. Paine made the case that no constitutional reform within the empire could solve the colonies’ grievances, because the problem was the system, not the personalities. Within months, colonial assemblies began authorising their delegates at the Second Congress to vote for independence.

Key Fact

Thomas Paine’s ‘Common Sense’, published January 1776, sold around 120,000 copies in three months in a population of 2.5 million. It attacked monarchy itself, not just the king’s ministers, and reframed independence as common sense for a continent.

Jefferson and the Declaration of Independence

On 7 June 1776 Richard Henry Lee of Virginia moved a resolution at the Second Congress ‘That these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.’ A drafting committee of five — John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, Robert Livingston and the thirty-three-year-old Virginia delegate Thomas Jefferson — was appointed to write a justification. Jefferson did most of the writing. His draft argued that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, that George III had broken that contract, and that ‘all men are created equal’ with rights to ‘life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness’. On 2 July 1776 Lee’s resolution passed; on 4 July 1776 the Congress approved Jefferson’s amended Declaration of Independence. Eighteenth-century broadside printers had it in every colonial newspaper within weeks.

Jefferson’s ‘all men are created equal’ was selective, and contemporary readers knew it. Jefferson himself enslaved more than 600 people across his lifetime. His original draft included a clause condemning the king for the transatlantic slave trade, but the Congress struck it out at the insistence of Southern delegates — especially South Carolina and Georgia. The final Declaration is silent on slavery. It is also hostile to Indigenous peoples, accusing the king of having ‘endeavoured to bring on the inhabitants of our frontiers, the merciless Indian Savages’. Holding both readings together — the Declaration as a landmark statement of natural rights and the Declaration as a document that erased the rights of enslaved people and Indigenous nations — is what a top-band judgement looks like in the unit’s final lesson.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Analytical Narrative on the road from Congress to independence, build a chain of causation rather than a list of meetings: the First Continental Congress’s Continental Association, Lexington and Concord, the Olive Branch Petition, the king’s rejection and the Prohibitory Act, ‘Common Sense’, the Lee resolution, the Declaration. Use causal connectives and show contingency — that reconciliation was still the goal as late as July 1775. For an 8-mark Explain the Importance question on Paine or Jefferson, anchor importance to specific developments: Paine’s 120,000 copies converting public opinion in three months; Jefferson’s draft framing independence in the language of natural rights that the next generation of reformers would invoke. Acknowledge that the Declaration was silent on slavery and hostile to Indigenous peoples — examiners reward this complication, not the celebratory reading.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First Continental Congress (Sept–Oct 1774) sought reconciliation through a Declaration of Rights and Grievances and a Continental Association boycott; the Second Congress (May 1775) became a wartime government, raising the Continental Army and trying the Olive Branch Petition before the king’s rejection forced the issue.
  • Thomas Paine’s ‘Common Sense’ (January 1776) attacked monarchy itself, framed independence as common sense for a continent, and converted mass public opinion in three months.
  • The Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), drafted by Thomas Jefferson, made the case for independence in the language of natural rights — while remaining silent on slavery and hostile to Indigenous peoples.

lessons.title: The War of Independence, 1775–83
lessons.description: Saratoga, Yorktown, Washington, British mistakes, French and Spanish help, the Peace of Paris.
lessons.content_html:
Why ‘Washington Won the War’ Is Not the Whole Story

When most students reach for an answer to ‘why did America win?’ they reach for George Washington. He matters — but the spec asks for four factors, not one: Washington’s leadership, British mistakes, French involvement and Spanish involvement. The decisive shift came in October 1777, when an American victory at Saratoga turned a colonial rebellion into a global war that Britain could not win on three oceans at once. Top-band answers weigh these factors against each other and reach a substantiated judgement, rather than ranking Washington first by default.

Key Fact

The specification names four factors in American victory: Washington’s leadership, British mistakes, French involvement, and Spanish involvement. A balanced answer weighs all four; reducing the war to Washington alone caps the answer in the lower bands.

Why Britain Expected a Quick War

In 1775 most ministers in London expected to crush the rebellion in a single campaigning season. Britain had the world’s largest navy, a professional army, and the financial resources of an empire. The colonies had no navy, no national treasury, no manufacturing base for muskets and powder, and a population of 2.5 million against Britain’s 8 million. Yet by 1781 Britain had lost. Three problems explain why. First, the strategic geography — armies that landed at New York or Charleston had to march hundreds of miles inland through forested country with no roads, while supplies came across an ocean three thousand miles wide. Second, British commanders frequently failed to coordinate; the early plan for 1777 collapsed when General Howe sailed for Philadelphia instead of moving up the Hudson to support General Burgoyne. Third, the Continental Army did not have to win battles; it only had to stay in the field long enough for British public patience to run out.

Saratoga, October 1777 — The Turning Point

The British plan for 1777 had General Burgoyne march south from Canada, General Howe move north up the Hudson and a third force come east from Lake Ontario, meeting at Albany to cut New England off from the other colonies. The plan unravelled. Howe took his army to Philadelphia. The third force was beaten back at Oriskany. Burgoyne pushed on alone through the Adirondack forest, slowed by his baggage train and harassed by militia. At Saratoga in upstate New York he was surrounded by an American force under Horatio Gates and Benedict Arnold. After two battles in September and October 1777, Burgoyne surrendered his army of around 6,000 on 17 October. The Battle of Saratoga was a turning point because of what it persuaded France to do.

French and Spanish Involvement

France had been quietly funnelling money, muskets and powder to the Americans since 1776, anxious to see Britain humiliated after the loss of Canada in 1763. After Saratoga the French foreign minister Vergennes signed two treaties at Paris on 6 February 1778: an alliance and a treaty of commerce. France was now an open belligerent. Spain followed in June 1779, allied to France though not formally to the United States. The Dutch joined the war against Britain in December 1780. What had begun as a colonial rebellion was now a global war from the West Indies to the English Channel to the Indian Ocean. Britain had to defend Gibraltar (besieged by Spain), Jamaica (threatened by France), Minorca (lost in 1782), and the home islands themselves — the Channel was briefly threatened by a combined Franco-Spanish fleet in 1779. Manpower and ships that could have crushed Washington had to be sent elsewhere.

A common student error is to centre the war on Washington’s leadership and treat French and Spanish help as a footnote. The specification weights all four factors, and the highest band rewards balance. Saratoga was an American victory commanded by Gates and Arnold, not Washington; the French alliance it produced added 12,000 troops at Yorktown and a French fleet that trapped Cornwallis; Spanish troops under Bernardo de Gálvez took the British forts at Mobile and Pensacola, opening a second front along the Gulf coast; the British surrendered at Yorktown to a combined Franco-American force under French command for the siege engineering. Higher-band answers explain how these factors interacted, rather than ranking Washington as the single decisive cause.

Washington’s Leadership and Valley Forge

If Washington did not win battles, why did the specification rank him alongside French intervention? Because in 1777–78 the Continental Army nearly disintegrated and his leadership prevented it. Around 11,000 troops wintered with Washington at Valley Forge in Pennsylvania between December 1777 and June 1778. Some 2,500 died of disease and exposure. Pay was months in arrears, food was so short that men ate ‘fire-cake’ (flour and water roasted on stones), and shoes were so scarce that some marches left bloody footprints in the snow. Washington kept the army together by argument, by personal example, and by accepting the help of the Prussian-trained Baron von Steuben in turning farmers into a drilled force capable of standing in line of battle. The army that emerged in spring 1778 was a different army. The British failure to destroy it during that winter was their largest single mistake of the war. Washington also chose, after 1776, a strategy of patience — avoiding pitched battles, harrying British supply lines, keeping the army intact rather than risking it on Continental-style fixed engagements.

Key Fact

Around 11,000 Continental troops wintered with Washington at Valley Forge in Pennsylvania from December 1777 to June 1778. About 2,500 died of disease and exposure. Baron von Steuben’s drilling that winter turned the survivors into a professional army.

The Southern Campaign and Yorktown, 1781

From 1779 the British shifted strategy southwards, hoping to mobilise loyalist support in Georgia and the Carolinas. They captured Savannah and Charleston, but were harassed by patriot militia and partisan leaders such as Francis Marion. In summer 1781 General Cornwallis marched his army into Yorktown on the Virginia coast and dug in to await resupply by sea. The French fleet under Admiral de Grasse beat off a British relief fleet at the Battle of the Chesapeake on 5 September 1781, leaving Cornwallis sealed off from the sea. Washington and the French commander Rochambeau brought their armies south. After a three-week siege Cornwallis surrendered around 7,000 men on 19 October 1781. News of the surrender forced Lord North’s government from office in March 1782. Britain’s new ministry under Lord Shelburne sought a settlement.

The specification asks students to weigh British mistakes alongside Washington and the European allies. The clearest examples are concrete and worth memorising. The 1777 plan that left Burgoyne unsupported because Howe sailed for Philadelphia handed the Americans Saratoga and the French alliance. The choice to launch a southern strategy from 1779 in the belief that Loyalists would rise in large numbers under-estimated how far patriot militia control had spread; the Loyalists who did fight (around 19,000 men over the war) were never the deciding force London hoped. Cornwallis’s decision to dig in at Yorktown without secure naval cover assumed a level of British command of the sea that the French fleet was about to deny him at the Chesapeake. Higher-band answers identify mistakes by name and link them to specific outcomes; lower-band answers say only that Britain ‘made mistakes’.

The Peace of Paris, 1783

The American negotiators were John Adams, John Jay and Benjamin Franklin. Franklin had been in Paris since 1776 and was the senior diplomat of the new republic. The Americans broke the terms of their alliance with France and negotiated separately with Britain, fearing that France and Spain would settle for a smaller American territory in order to win their own concessions. The Peace of Paris, signed on 3 September 1783, was generous to the United States: Britain recognised independence, ceded all territory east of the Mississippi between the Great Lakes and Florida, and granted American fishermen access to the Newfoundland banks. Franklin’s personal standing in Paris and his coolness in negotiation helped secure these terms. Spain regained Florida and Minorca; France gained almost nothing for its trouble and was left with vast debts that contributed to its own revolution in 1789.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain the Importance question on Saratoga, anchor importance to French entry into the war: the French treaties of February 1778 turned a colonial rebellion into a global war that Britain had to fight on three oceans. For an 8-mark Analytical Narrative on why America won, build a chain that weighs all four factors — Washington keeping the Continental Army intact at Valley Forge, British failure to coordinate Burgoyne and Howe in 1777, French troops and ships at Yorktown, Spanish opening of a Gulf-coast front under Gálvez. Use causal connectives. Avoid the trap of ranking Washington as the single cause: examiners reward balanced multi-factor analysis, especially the international dimension. For an Importance question on the Peace of Paris, point to Franklin’s diplomatic standing and the territorial settlement east of the Mississippi.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Saratoga (October 1777) was the turning point because the surrender of Burgoyne’s 6,000 men brought France into the war as an open ally in February 1778, with Spain following in 1779.
  • Washington’s leadership mattered most at Valley Forge (winter 1777–78), where his refusal to let the Continental Army disintegrate and Baron von Steuben’s drilling produced the professional force that fought the war’s second half.
  • Yorktown (October 1781) ended major fighting when a combined Franco-American force trapped Cornwallis on the Virginia coast; the Peace of Paris (1783), negotiated by Franklin, recognised American independence and ceded territory east of the Mississippi.

lessons.title: Consequences: Slavery, Indigenous Peoples and Loyalists
lessons.description: Slavery after independence, the cost to Indigenous peoples, and Loyalist exile to Canada.
lessons.content_html:
Who Actually Won?

The Declaration of Independence proclaimed that ‘all men are created equal’. The Peace of Paris ceded the United States territory the size of Western Europe. Yet for three groups the war was a defeat dressed as victory. Around half a million enslaved African Americans remained enslaved after independence, and the Constitution of 1787 entrenched that slavery in federal law. Indigenous nations, having mostly backed Britain to defend their lands, were treated by the new United States as a defeated people whose territory was forfeit. And around 60,000 Loyalists were forced into exile. Holding all three groups in view, alongside the celebrated story of patriot triumph, is what a balanced judgement on the unit looks like in the highest band.

Key Fact

The war’s consequences cut three ways: enslaved African Americans (around half a million remained enslaved despite Northern abolition); Indigenous peoples (treated by the new republic as defeated and dispossessed); and around 60,000 Loyalists (driven into exile, mostly to Nova Scotia and the Niagara region).

Independence and Slavery: A Two-Speed Settlement

In the Northern states, the rhetoric of liberty did push abolition forward, but slowly. Vermont’s 1777 constitution was the first in the world to ban adult slavery. Pennsylvania passed a Gradual Abolition Act in 1780; Massachusetts ended slavery through a series of court rulings in 1781–83 (notably the Quock Walker case); New York and New Jersey passed gradual emancipation laws in 1799 and 1804. Most freed children only on reaching adulthood, and many enslaved people were sold south before that deadline. In the Southern states the opposite happened. The cotton boom of the 1790s entrenched the plantation system. The 1787 Constitution’s three-fifths clause counted three out of every five enslaved people for the purpose of representation in Congress — giving slaveholding states more votes without granting any to the enslaved. The same Constitution forbade Congress from ending the transatlantic slave trade before 1808. The new United States legalised the regional split that the Civil War would eventually fight over.

Black Loyalists and the Promise of Freedom

Many enslaved people read the war differently from white patriots. In November 1775 Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, proclaimed freedom to any enslaved man who would join the British forces. Around 800 men responded. Sir Henry Clinton’s Philipsburg Proclamation of 1779 widened the offer to any enslaved person of either sex who reached British lines. Tens of thousands ran. When the British evacuated New York in 1783 the navy carried away around 3,000 free Black Loyalists in what became known as the Book of Negroes — a meticulous register of their names and former enslavers. Most settled in Nova Scotia. They received less land than white Loyalists, faced segregation and a violent race riot at Shelburne in 1784. In 1792 around 1,200 dissatisfied Black Loyalists migrated under the leadership of Thomas Peters and the Sierra Leone Company to found the colony of Freetown in West Africa — the first organised return to Africa by people of African descent in the Atlantic world.

A common error is to write enslaved people as objects of policy — freed by Vermont, kept in chains by Virginia — rather than as historical agents. Tens of thousands ran to British lines in response to Dunmore’s proclamation, the largest single act of resistance to slavery in colonial America. The Black Loyalists who reached Nova Scotia, the founders of Freetown, the Quaker abolitionists who lobbied state legislatures, and the petitioners to the Massachusetts courts all show enslaved people and free Black Americans shaping their own settlement. Higher-band answers acknowledge this agency. Lower-band answers reduce slavery to a Southern institution that white politicians decided about.

Consequences for Indigenous Peoples

Most Indigenous nations had judged that British policy — the 1763 Proclamation Line restricting white settlement — offered better protection of their lands than the patriot cause. The Iroquois Confederacy split, with the Mohawk under Joseph Brant joining the British, while the Oneida and Tuscarora supported the Americans. Cherokee, Creek and Shawnee fought British alliances. The Peace of Paris of 1783 ignored them entirely: Britain ceded territory east of the Mississippi to the United States without consulting the nations who lived there. The new United States treated Indigenous peoples as a defeated people whose lands were forfeit. Treaties signed under duress at Fort Stanwix (1784), Fort McIntosh (1785) and Fort Finney (1786) extracted vast cessions. Pro-British Iroquois under Joseph Brant moved north of the Great Lakes into the Niagara region on land granted by the Crown — the Haldimand Tract of around 950,000 acres along the Grand River, where the Six Nations Reserve still exists today. The war that produced American independence was, for most Indigenous nations, a catastrophe.

Key Fact

Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea) led pro-British Mohawks and other Iroquois after the war to the Haldimand Tract in the Niagara region — around 950,000 acres along the Grand River granted by the British Crown in 1784.

The Loyalists: Persecution and Exile

Around one in five colonists had remained loyal to the Crown, with stronger Loyalist communities in the middle colonies and the South. During the war Loyalists faced confiscation of property, tar-and-feathering, and trial by patriot Committees of Safety. After the war state legislatures passed Confiscation Acts that seized Loyalist estates. The Peace of Paris asked Congress to ‘recommend’ restitution but did not require it; in practice almost no property was returned. About 60,000 to 80,000 Loyalists went into exile. Around 30,000 white Loyalists settled in Nova Scotia and the new Canadian colony of New Brunswick (carved out in 1784 to accommodate them). Others moved to Quebec, the Niagara peninsula in what became Upper Canada (1791), the British West Indies, or Britain itself. Black Loyalists made up around 3,000 of the Nova Scotia settlers. The British government paid around £3 million in compensation through the Loyalist Claims Commission — substantial, though far less than was claimed.

Historians have not agreed on how to weigh the war’s consequences. The traditional Whig reading, developed in the nineteenth century and revived by Bernard Bailyn, frames the Revolution as a triumph of natural rights ideology with consequences that took longer to work through but reached enslaved people and women in the long nineteenth century. Progressive historians like Charles Beard read the same documents as the work of a propertied elite securing their own economic interests. More recent ‘history from below’ writing, including Gary Nash’s ‘The Unknown American Revolution’, foregrounds working people, enslaved people and Indigenous nations — for whom independence delivered no rights at all in 1783. GCSE answers do not need to name historians, but a brief ‘historians have disagreed’ framing in a judgement helps unlock the highest band on a balanced verdict.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain the Importance question on the war’s consequences, anchor importance to specific developments — the three-fifths clause embedding slavery in the 1787 Constitution; Joseph Brant’s migration to the Haldimand Tract along the Grand River; the British government’s £3 million paid through the Loyalist Claims Commission. For an 8-mark Analytical Narrative on consequences, build a chain that shows how each group’s experience flowed from a specific decision: the Peace of Paris ceding territory east of the Mississippi without consulting Indigenous nations; the Confiscation Acts driving Loyalist exile to Nova Scotia and the Niagara region; Northern gradual emancipation laws contrasting with the cotton-boom entrenchment of Southern slavery. Use causal connectives. Treat enslaved people and Indigenous peoples as historical agents, not as objects of policy — examiners reward this framing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Northern states moved towards abolition (Vermont 1777, Pennsylvania 1780, Massachusetts 1781–83) but Southern states entrenched slavery, and the 1787 Constitution’s three-fifths clause and 1808 slave-trade clause built that division into federal law.
  • Most Indigenous nations had backed Britain to protect their lands; the Peace of Paris ignored them, and Joseph Brant led pro-British Mohawks to the Haldimand Tract along the Grand River in the Niagara region.
  • Around 60,000 to 80,000 Loyalists, including 3,000 Black Loyalists, were driven into exile, mostly to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; around £3 million was paid in compensation by the British government.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of American independence for the institution of slavery in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: independence led directly to a wave of Northern abolition laws — Vermont (1777), Pennsylvania’s Gradual Abolition Act (1780) and the Massachusetts court rulings (1781–83) — that began to divide the new republic into free and slave states; it also led to the 1787 Constitution’s three-fifths clause, which counted three out of every five enslaved people for representation, giving slaveholding states extra political weight in Congress while granting the enslaved no rights at all. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to abolition laws or the Constitution.
Emerging: Notes that slavery existed without showing how independence shaped it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of American independence for the position of Indigenous peoples in North America.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: independence mattered because the Peace of Paris of 1783 ceded territory east of the Mississippi to the United States without consulting the Indigenous nations who lived there, removing the protection that the 1763 Proclamation Line had offered; it also mattered because the new United States treated Indigenous peoples as a defeated people whose lands were forfeit, extracting cessions through treaties under duress at Fort Stanwix (1784) and Fort McIntosh (1785). A third anchor might be the migration of Joseph Brant’s Mohawks to the Haldimand Tract in the Niagara region. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus.
Emerging: Mentions Indigenous peoples without explaining how independence affected them.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the war for the Loyalists.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: state Confiscation Acts after the war seized Loyalist estates with little prospect of restitution despite the Peace of Paris recommending it, driving around 60,000 to 80,000 colonists into exile; resettlement schemes carried around 30,000 white Loyalists and 3,000 Black Loyalists to Nova Scotia, with New Brunswick carved out as a separate colony in 1784 to accommodate them and the Niagara peninsula receiving others under what became Upper Canada in 1791. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to confiscation or resettlement.
Emerging: Mentions Loyalists without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Black Loyalists for the post-war settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: the Black Loyalists mattered because tens of thousands of enslaved people had run to British lines after Dunmore’s 1775 proclamation and Clinton’s 1779 Philipsburg Proclamation, the largest single act of resistance to slavery in colonial America; their evacuation in the 1783 Book of Negroes mattered because around 3,000 free Black Loyalists were carried to Nova Scotia, where their experience of inferior land grants and the 1784 Shelburne riot drove around 1,200 of them to migrate under Thomas Peters in 1792 to found Freetown in Sierra Leone — the first organised return to Africa by people of African descent in the Atlantic world. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions Black Loyalists without showing the wider significance.
Emerging: General references to enslaved people without specific examples.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how the war shaped the lives of enslaved people, Indigenous peoples and Loyalists in the years 1775–83. You may use the following information in your answer:
• Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation (1775)
• The Haldimand Tract
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains how each group’s experience flowed from specific decisions rather than narrating in sequence. Links Dunmore’s 1775 proclamation and Clinton’s 1779 Philipsburg Proclamation to the flight of tens of thousands of enslaved people and the Black Loyalist evacuation of 1783; links the Iroquois split, Joseph Brant’s alliance with Britain, and the post-war Haldimand Tract to the dispossession of Indigenous nations on the American side of the new border; brings in own knowledge such as the Confiscation Acts, the three-fifths clause, the Loyalist Claims Commission, or the Vermont and Pennsylvania abolition laws. Reaches an analytical judgement about who actually won.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis.
Emerging: Lists groups without explaining how the war shaped their experience.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the 1787 United States Constitution for the future of slavery in the new republic.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: the three-fifths clause mattered because it counted three out of every five enslaved people for representation in Congress, giving the slaveholding states a permanent political bonus that protected slavery from federal abolition; the 1808 slave-trade clause mattered because it forbade Congress from ending the transatlantic slave trade for twenty years, allowing tens of thousands more Africans to be enslaved before the door closed. A third anchor might be the contrast with the Northern abolition laws of the same period, which made the Constitution’s pro-slavery provisions a regional fault line that the Civil War would eventually fight over. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions the Constitution without showing how it shaped slavery.
Emerging: General references to slavery without specific examples.
